Magnetosphere

Words: 95 Articles: 1
Planetary science OurBigBook.com
A magnetosphere is the region around a body in which the body's magnetic interaction controls charged-particle motion and its response to the surrounding plasma. A planet with an intrinsic magnetic field can support a compressed dayside and an extended magnetotail in the solar wind. Magnetospheric currents must be distinguished from the internal field when inferring a planetary dynamo.

Induced magnetosphere

Words: 41
Magnetosphere OurBigBook.com
An induced magnetosphere is maintained by the interaction of an external magnetized plasma flow with a conducting ionosphere or atmosphere. Its currents and draped magnetic field do not establish an internal planetary dynamo. Venus is a central example; Mars combines this interaction with localized crustal fields.

Planetary magnetic field

Words: 228 Articles: 3
Planetary science OurBigBook.com
A planetary magnetic field may include an intrinsic field maintained by an internal planetary dynamo, local crustal remanent magnetization, and externally driven fields associated with the solar wind. Separating these components requires spatial and temporal observations. A global internally sourced field, a localized crustal anomaly, and an induced magnetosphere are different evidence about the planet's present and past interior.

Planetary dynamo

Words: 174 Articles: 2
Planetary magnetic field OurBigBook.com
A planetary dynamo maintains an intrinsic magnetic field by motion of an electrically conducting fluid. The resistive induction equation balances stretching and transport against magnetic diffusion. A sufficiently large magnetic Reynolds number is necessary but does not ensure that the flow regenerates every required field component. Thermal or compositional convection supplies mechanical power; rotation organizes the flow through the Coriolis force, and the Lorentz force density eventually modifies the flow and limits growth. A fluid core can fail to operate a dynamo if it is stably stratified or inadequately driven.

Geodynamo

Words: 63
Planetary dynamo OurBigBook.com
The geodynamo is the maintenance of Earth's magnetic field by electrically conducting fluid motion in its liquid outer core. Rotation and buoyant convection organize helical flow and permit mean-field poloidal–toroidal regeneration. A scalar homogeneous alpha model explains a mechanism and a threshold but omits spherical boundaries, anisotropy, spatial variations and Lorentz force feedback. Reversals and saturation require dynamical or time-dependent transport information beyond a growing constant-coefficient kinematic mode.

Geomagnetic reversal

Words: 35
Planetary dynamo OurBigBook.com
A geomagnetic reversal changes the large-scale polarity of Earth's intrinsic magnetic field. Crustal remanent magnetization records past reversals. The reversal times are not a regular clock; their occurrence reflects time-dependent dynamo action rather than rigid rotation of a permanent magnet.

Asteroid

Words: 33
Planetary science OurBigBook.com
An asteroid is a small rocky or metallic body orbiting a star. Asteroid dynamics can involve mean-motion resonances, planetary scattering and secular perturbations. Solar-system asteroids illustrate how phase protection can prevent close encounters even when orbital paths approach a planet.

Astronomical unit (AU)

Words: 33
Planetary science OurBigBook.com
The astronomical unit is a length scale used for Solar System distances, approximately 1.5×1013cm. Coarse estimates sometimes round it to 1013cm. Numerical coefficients in planet formation estimates depend on which approximation is used.

Planet formation

Words: 145 Articles: 3
Planetary science OurBigBook.com

Core accretion

Words: 35
Planet formation OurBigBook.com
Core accretion forms a planet by building a solid core through growth and accretion of solid material. A sufficiently massive core can then bind a gaseous envelope. It is distinct from direct fragmentation through gravitational instability of an astrophysical disk.

Minimum-mass solar nebula

Words: 58
Planet formation OurBigBook.com
The minimum-mass solar nebula estimates a primordial gas-and-solid protoplanetary disk by spreading planetary material into annuli and restoring a solar mixture. A common idealized surface density is proportional to r−3/2. This reconstruction is a model of minimum material requirements, not a unique history of the Solar System. Extrapolating it far beyond the planetary region need not give a physically consistent disk.

Hot and cold starts of a giant planet (s0​)

Words: 52
Planet formation OurBigBook.com
Accretion releases gravitational energy. Efficient radiation at an accretion shock leaves a lower-entropy cold start, while greater retained energy gives a higher-entropy hot start; intermediate outcomes are possible. Initial entropy changes a young planet's radius, luminosity and spectrum. Consequently an exoplanet direct imaging luminosity and age need not uniquely fix mass without a formation/evolution model.

Comet

Planetary science OurBigBook.com

Comet tail

Words: 87 Articles: 1
Comet OurBigBook.com
A comet tail is an extended structure formed from material released by a comet. Its dust tail is shaped largely by radiation pressure, while an ion tail is shaped by the solar wind and magnetic field. The cometary dust tail is the solid-grain component.

Cometary dust tail

Words: 47
Comet tail OurBigBook.com
A cometary dust tail is the extended distribution of solid grains released by a comet. Radiation pressure sorts its grains by size: high-β grains are displaced rapidly in the anti-stellar direction, while larger low-β grains remain closer to the projected orbit and form a more curved trail.

Comet OurBigBook.com
With uniformly distributed apsidal orientations, the phase-mixed radial probability of a Kepler orbit gives the surface probability per comet
Σc​(r)=π2(Q+q)(r−q)(Q−r)​1​.
(1)
For Q≫r>q, this is π−2Q−3/2r−1/2(1−q/r)−1/2. Multiply by the population size for a number surface density of a disk.

Planet

Planetary science OurBigBook.com

Mercury (planet)

Words: 36
Planet OurBigBook.com
The innermost planet has a large metallic core and a weak but global intrinsic magnetic field. Its observed field supports an active planetary dynamo in a fluid conducting part of that core. Slow rotation does not by itself exclude dynamo action.

Terrestrial planet

Words: 29
Planet OurBigBook.com
A planet dominated by rocky and metallic material rather than a massive H/He envelope. Earth and Mars are examples. A super-Earth is a mass category and need not be a terrestrial planet.

Ice giant

Words: 41
Planet OurBigBook.com
A giant planet with a much larger heavy-element fraction than a typical gas giant, exemplified by Uranus and Neptune. Water, ammonia and other volatile-rich materials are called “ices” in formation terminology; they need not remain ordinary frozen solids in the hot deep interior.

Gas giant

Words: 38
Planet OurBigBook.com
A large planet whose bulk mass includes a substantial hydrogen–helium envelope, as in Jupiter and Saturn. The deep envelope is fluid rather than a dilute atmosphere with a sharp solid surface. Its cooling, compression and possible electron degeneracy pressure influence the mass-radius relation.

Earth's outer core

Words: 45
Earth OurBigBook.com
Earth's outer core is a liquid, electrically conducting region whose buoyant motion and rotation sustain the geodynamo. Its magnetic field both responds to the flow through induction and modifies that flow through the Lorentz force. A prescribed-velocity kinematic model describes onset rather than the entire nonlinear core dynamics.

Terrestrial atmosphere

Words: 134 Articles: 4
Earth OurBigBook.com
The terrestrial atmosphere has regions with opposite signs of the atmospheric lapse rate: the troposphere usually cools upward, the stratosphere warms upward through ultraviolet heating, the mesosphere cools, and the thermosphere warms. A monotone atmospheric pressure-temperature profile can approximate one such interval, but cannot describe all their transitions with one fixed branch.
Thermosphere
Words: 32
Terrestrial atmosphere OurBigBook.com
The thermosphere is a high atmospheric region where absorption of energetic stellar radiation can produce an upward-rising kinetic temperature. Its very low density distinguishes kinetic temperature from a large thermal energy content.
Mesosphere
Words: 14
Terrestrial atmosphere OurBigBook.com
The mesosphere lies above the stratosphere and below the thermosphere. Its typical terrestrial temperature decreases upward.
Stratosphere
Words: 18
Terrestrial atmosphere OurBigBook.com
The terrestrial stratosphere lies above the troposphere and has an upward-warming region associated with ultraviolet heating by the ozone layer.
Troposphere
Words: 27
Terrestrial atmosphere OurBigBook.com
The troposphere is the lowest main layer of the terrestrial atmosphere, with weather and generally decreasing temperature with altitude. Local inversions and moist convection complicate a single lapse-rate description.

Rogue planet

Words: 31
Planet OurBigBook.com
A rogue planet has no bound host star. Without stellar irradiation, its luminosity can still be supplied by internal cooling and Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction; its emitting temperature need not equal the negligible irradiation-based planetary equilibrium temperature.

Natural satellite

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Planetary science OurBigBook.com
A natural satellite is a naturally occurring body orbiting a planet or another nonstellar body. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite; its synchronous rotation provides a familiar example of tidal locking.

Moon

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Natural satellite OurBigBook.com
The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. Its synchronous rotation keeps approximately the same near side of the Moon facing Earth, while both the near side of the Moon and the far side of the Moon experience sunlight and darkness. See illumination of a synchronously rotating moon for the geometry. [ref].

Near side of the Moon

Words: 26
Moon OurBigBook.com
The near side of the Moon is the hemisphere directed approximately toward Earth. Libration changes the exact visible boundary, so synchronous rotation does not mean that an observer always sees precisely the same hemisphere.

Far side of the Moon

Words: 39
Moon OurBigBook.com
The far side of the Moon is the hemisphere directed approximately away from Earth. “Far” describes the direction to Earth; it does not describe illumination by the Sun. The far side of the Moon experiences both sunlight and darkness during the lunar phase cycle. [ref].

Lunar phase

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Moon OurBigBook.com
A lunar phase is the appearance of the sunlit portion of the Moon as seen from Earth. Outside a lunar eclipse, the distant Sun illuminates approximately one hemisphere of the Moon, but an observer sees a changing overlap of that hemisphere with the hemisphere facing Earth. The lunar phase therefore changes even though synchronous rotation keeps approximately the same near side of the Moon facing Earth. [ref].
The cycle runs through new Moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full Moon, waning gibbous, last quarter and waning crescent. “Waxing” means that the lunar illuminated fraction is increasing; “waning” means it is decreasing. A crescent has less than half its apparent disk sunlit, and a gibbous lunar phase has more than half. First and last quarter each show half a disk: “quarter” refers to progress around the cycle, rather than a quarter of the disk being lit. [ref].
An instructive circular orbit model puts Earth at the origin, the Sun far away along +x, and the Moon at R(cosθ,sinθ). The sunward position x>0, θ=0, gives new Moon; the opposite position x<0, θ=π, gives full Moon. Counterclockwise motion gives first quarter at θ=π/2 and last quarter at θ=3π/2. The Sun's direction is fixed during this snapshot of the cycle. Every small globe in the orbital view is illuminated on its +x half; the adjacent apparent disks are separate views from Earth, rather than globes viewed from above.
The disk views choose north up, with the upward direction perpendicular to the orbital plane. In this convention waxing lunar phases are bright on the right and waning lunar phases on the left. Local horizon orientation and viewing from different locations on Earth can rotate the apparent disk; its lit edge always points toward the projected direction of the Sun. The lunar illuminated fraction is unaffected by this rotation.
The useful angle is the phase angle α=∠SME, with S the Sun, M the Moon and E the observer at Earth's center: its vertex is at the Moon. Full Moon has α=0, quarter has α=π/2, and new Moon has α=π in the ideal model. By contrast, the elongation ϵ=∠SEM has its vertex at Earth. For a distant Sun, its rays are parallel, so
α=π−ϵ,k=21+cosα​=21−cosϵ​.
(2)
Here k is the lunar illuminated fraction: a fraction of projected disk area, not a fraction of the Moon's total surface area or its received radiant flux relative to full Moon. The phase angle and unsigned elongation each lie between 0 and π, so either alone gives the illuminated amount without distinguishing waxing from waning. The orbital direction resolves that ambiguity.
The lunar illuminated fraction has an elegant geometric derivation. Model the Moon as a sphere of unit radius and view it along the z direction. Take the Sun's unit direction to be (sinα,0,cosα). A visible surface point above apparent disk coordinates (x,y) has z=1−x2−y2​. Direct illumination requires the outward normal's dot product with the sunward direction to be positive. The day-night terminator therefore obeys xsinα+zcosα=0. At a fixed y, set q=1−y2​; the visible day-night terminator is xt​=−qcosα, and the illuminated strip extends from xt​ to the right edge q. Integrating its width gives
Alit​=∫−11​(1+cosα)1−y2​dy=2π​(1+cosα),k=πAlit​​.
(3)
The integral is the area of half a unit circle. Thus a three-dimensional visibility problem reduces to a circle's area and a cosine. The derivation assumes parallel sunlight, a distant observer and a sphere, and ignores a lunar eclipse. Real observed brightness additionally depends on surface scattering of light and observing geometry, so k=1/2 does not promise half the full-Moon radiant flux.
For a worked example, elongation ϵ=60∘ gives phase angle α=120∘ and k=(1+cos120∘)/2=1/4: a crescent with 25% of its apparent disk sunlit. At elongation 120∘, the phase angle is 60∘ and k=3/4: a gibbous lunar phase. At 90∘, k=1/2. In each case the same k occurs once while waxing and once while waning in the ideal cycle.
Ordinary lunar phases are not caused by Earth's shadow. A lunar eclipse occurs only when the Moon actually enters that shadow near full Moon. The orbital inclination of the Moon is about 5∘ relative to Earth's orbital plane around the Sun; most full Moons pass above or below the shadow. This is why full Moon does not imply a lunar eclipse every month. [ref].
The phase cycle is a synodic month, about 29.5 days, whereas the Moon's orbital period relative to distant stars is a sidereal month, about 27.3 days. During one sidereal month, Earth advances around the Sun, so the Moon must move farther to repeat the sunward alignment. For coplanar circular orbits traversed in the same direction, subtract their mean motions: nsyn​=nsid​−nyear​, with n=2π/P. Hence
Psyn​1​=Psid​1​−Pyear​1​,Psyn​=Pyear​−Psid​Psid​Pyear​​.
(4)
Using Psid​=27.321661days and Pyear​=365.256days gives Psyn​=29.530591days, consistent with the mean synodic month of 29.53059 days. After one sidereal month, the sunward direction has advanced about 26.93∘; catching up takes about 2.21 more days. These are mean-period estimates: orbital eccentricity and changing geometry make individual synodic months vary. [ref]. [ref].
The lunar phase is also a practical clock for observing. Full Moon is opposite the Sun and rises roughly at sunset; first quarter is about a right angle from the Sun and is convenient in the evening, while last quarter is convenient before dawn. These are rough guides, not exact rise-time predictions for every place and season. [ref]. Historically, repeated lunar phases provided the month in lunar calendars, while half-lit disks gave Aristarchus of Samos a way to infer astronomical distances. [ref].
Phase angle (astronomy, α)
Words: 47
Lunar phase OurBigBook.com
The astronomical phase angle is the angle at an illuminated body between the directions to its light source and to its observer. For a lunar phase it is the Sun–Moon–observer angle at the Moon, rather than the elongation measured at Earth. A small phase angle gives a nearly full apparent disk in the spherical model.
Elongation (astronomy, ϵ)
Words: 48
Lunar phase OurBigBook.com
Elongation is the apparent angular separation of a celestial body from the Sun, measured at the observer. For a lunar phase, the elongation is the Sun–Earth–Moon angle; in the distant-Sun approximation it is supplementary to the phase angle. A given unsigned elongation can occur on either side of the Sun in the sky.
Lunar illuminated fraction (k)
Words: 58
Lunar phase OurBigBook.com
The lunar illuminated fraction is the directly sunlit projected area of the apparent lunar disk divided by its total projected area. For a sphere with parallel sunlight and a distant observer, outside a lunar eclipse, it is k=(1+cosα)/2, with phase angle α at the Moon. It measures geometry rather than the fraction of full-Moon radiant flux. [ref].
Sidereal month (Psid​)
Words: 44
Lunar phase OurBigBook.com
A sidereal month is the Moon's orbital period relative to distant stars, about 27.32166 days. It is shorter than the synodic month because the sunward direction changes as Earth travels around the Sun. The lunar spin period associated with synchronous rotation matches the sidereal month in the mean. [ref].
Synodic month (Psyn​)
Words: 54
Lunar phase OurBigBook.com
A synodic month is the synodic period of the Moon relative to the Sun, about 29.53059 days on average. A lunation is commonly measured from one new Moon to the next. Actual lunations vary, so the constant-speed relation derived in lunar phase is useful for understanding the mean cycle rather than predicting exact dates. [ref].
Aristarchus of Samos
Words: 136
Lunar phase OurBigBook.com
Aristarchus of Samos used the half-lit Moon to estimate the relative distances of the Sun and Moon. In the spherical illumination model a half-lit disk means phase angle α=π/2, so the Sun–Moon–Earth triangle is right-angled at the Moon. Keeping the Sun at a finite distance, let dEM​ and dES​ be the distances from Earth to the Moon and Sun. Then elongation ϵ at Earth gives
cosϵ=dES​dEM​​,dEM​dES​​=cosϵ1​.
(5)
The 87∘ elongation attributed to Aristarchus of Samos gives a ratio about 19.1, consistent with his conclusion that the Sun was between 18 and 20 times farther away. The example shows how lunar phase geometry becomes a distance measurement, but the ratio is extremely sensitive to an angle close to 90∘. Unlike the distant-Sun approximation, this finite triangle has elongation slightly less than 90∘ at half illumination. [ref].

Lunar eclipse

Words: 44
Moon OurBigBook.com
A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth blocks some or all of the direct sunlight reaching the Moon. It requires alignment near full Moon; the orbital inclination usually carries the Moon clear of Earth's shadow. Ordinary lunar phases instead arise from viewing different amounts of the sunlit hemisphere. [ref].

Libration

Words: 88
Moon OurBigBook.com
Libration is the apparent rocking of a body as seen by an observer. Planetary system dynamics OurBigBook.com
Tidal locking settles a body's spin into a sustained relation with its orbital motion through tidal forces and tidal dissipation. The simplest case is synchronous rotation, a 1:1 spin-orbit resonance. On an ideal circular orbit, with spin axis perpendicular to the orbital plane, the body keeps the same face toward its companion, as the Moon approximately does toward Earth. [ref].
This article retains the broader sense of tidal locking as capture into a spin-orbit resonance; the term is also commonly used specifically for synchronous rotation. Tidally evolved rotation need not be 1:1: Mercury has a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance with the Sun, turning three times in two orbital periods. The distinction matters when inferring illumination or climate from a spin period. [ref].

The familiar two-bulge picture represents an elongated response along the companion direction, rather than a separate force pulling only the nearest surface. If spin and orbital motion differ, the forcing sweeps through the body's material. With tidal dissipation, the response is out of alignment with the instantaneous forcing, allowing a net torque. Tidal locking OurBigBook.com
A secular tidal torque is the torque remaining after averaging the changing tidal interaction over fast orbital and rotational motion. The misaligned tidal deformation lets the companion's gravity change the spin angular momentum; the orbit receives the opposite torque. Tidal dissipation converts mechanical energy into heat, while total angular momentum is conserved in an isolated system. Thus the spin-orbit coupling exchanges angular momentum rather than destroying it. [ref].
For intuition near synchronous rotation on a circular orbit, hold mean motion n and moment of inertia I fixed and adopt the illustrative linear dissipative law
Iω˙=⟨τ⟩=−K(ω−n),K>0,ω=θ˙.
(6)
Here ω is spin angular velocity, θ is a marked surface direction in an inertial frame, and K is a response coefficient, not a universal material constant. A faster spin is slowed and a slower prograde spin is accelerated. The solution and the associated mechanical power loss are
ω(t)−n=[ω(0)−n]e−Kt/I,E˙mech​=⟨τ⟩(ω−n)=−K(ω−n)2≤0.
(7)
The orbital contribution to this power is −n⟨τ⟩, and the spin contribution is ω⟨τ⟩; their sum becomes heat. Holding n fixed is a local approximation to the coupled evolution. Actual secular tidal torque depends on the deformation response and orbital eccentricity, so this simple law does not establish which spin-orbit resonance an eccentric body captures into.

Synchronous rotation is 1:1; Mercury's 3:2 spin-orbit resonance is nonsynchronous. The relevant combination of spin and orbital angles must stay bounded around a preferred orientation, not merely have a near-integer frequency ratio. For an elongated body on an eccentric orbit, the companion's gravitational torque on the permanent shape can sustain the resonance while tidal dissipation permits capture. [ref].

Synchronous rotation means one prograde turn about the body's own axis per orbital period, measured against fixed directions in an inertial frame. This 1:1 spin-orbit resonance approximately describes the Moon's synchronous rotation toward Earth. [ref].
The striking geometric idea is that one turn in space can keep one face toward the companion: a fixed orientation in the frame turning with the orbit is a changing orientation in an inertial frame. This distinction helps us predict illumination: a synchronously rotating exoplanet orbiting its illuminating star can have persistent day and night hemispheres, whereas the Moon, synchronized to Earth, receives changing illumination from a different body, the Sun.

The Moon keeps its near side of the Moon approximately toward Earth, while the direction to the distant Sun is nearly fixed during the idealized orbit shown below. A fixed surface patch therefore turns toward, across and away from sunlight. The far side of the Moon has day and night too; its name does not mean permanent darkness. [ref].
If the Sun direction has fixed angle α and the marked surface patch has outward normal vector at angle θ, its direct illumination is proportional to max(0,cos(θ−α)). With synchronous rotation, θ=f+π, so the patch goes through day and night even though it always faces Earth. In reality the Earth-Moon system advances around the Sun: the lunar spin and orbital cycle relative to distant stars is about 27.3 Earth days, while the lunar phase cycle has a synodic period of about 29.5 Earth days. These numbers describe the actual system, not the fixed-sunlight cartoon. [ref].
For a synchronously rotating exoplanet whose orbital companion is itself the illuminating star, the direction to the star turns with the orbit. On an ideal circular orbit, with perpendicular spin axis and no additional oscillations, this direction is fixed relative to the surface, giving persistent day and night hemispheres. Day-night heat redistribution then helps determine the nightside temperature; permanent lack of direct starlight does not imply zero temperature. Orbital eccentricity and departures from this ideal spin geometry modify that simple picture.

Radiation-pressure coefficient (β)

Interplanetary dust OurBigBook.com
The radiation-pressure coefficient is the ratio of outward stellar radiation pressure to inward stellar gravity on a dust grain. The grain therefore feels effective gravitational parameter (1−β)GM∗​.

Dust orbit released from a circular parent ring

Words: 34
Radiation-pressure coefficient OurBigBook.com
If release imparts no velocity kick, a grain's initial Kepler orbit under reduced stellar attraction has q=rb​, Q=rb​/(1−2β), and e=β/(1−β) for 0≤β<1/2. Its pericentre distance remains at the dust birth ring, while its apocentre distance grows with the radiation-pressure coefficient.

Radiation-pressure efficiency (Qpr​)

Words: 38
Radiation-pressure coefficient OurBigBook.com
The radiation-pressure efficiency is the radiation-force cross-section of a grain divided by its geometric cross-section. It is of order unity for grains larger than the illuminating wavelength and depends strongly on size and composition in the small-particle regime.

Radiation-pressure blowout orbit

Words: 85 Articles: 1
Radiation-pressure coefficient OurBigBook.com
A grain released from a circular parent orbit without a relative velocity impulse is unbound when radiation pressure reduces the effective stellar attraction sufficiently. For β>1, the effective inverse-square force is repulsive.
Radiation-pressure blowout threshold (β=1/2)
Words: 52
Radiation-pressure blowout orbit OurBigBook.com
The zero-kick circular-parent threshold is β=1/2: below it grains are initially bound, at it their conservative release orbit is parabolic, and above it they are initially unbound. Poynting–Robertson drag can modify a marginal orbit, so the threshold is a statement about the instantaneous release orbit, not an exact capture criterion with dissipation included.

A synchrone is the locus, at one observation time, of grains released at the same time with different radiation-pressure coefficients.

A syndyne is the locus, at one observation time, of grains with the same radiation-pressure coefficient released at different times.

Poynting–Robertson drag

Words: 676 Articles: 10
Interplanetary dust OurBigBook.com
Poynting–Robertson drag is the tangential component of stellar radiation force caused by aberration in an orbiting dust grain's frame. It removes orbital energy and angular momentum and drives the grain inward.

For grains of fixed diameter D released instantaneously at r0​, the drift law r˙=−γ/(rD) integrates to the displayed size-radius map. The time to radius r<r0​ is tr​(D)=D(r02​−r2)/(2γ). Grains therefore arrive in increasing diameter order. This model of Poynting–Robertson drag assumes nearly circular Kepler orbits, fixed positive γ, and no grain loss or diameter changes before arrival. At a positive time, the map is monotone in D and allows the initial power-law size distribution to be transformed into a spatial distribution or an arrival-time distribution.

Set Tr​=tr​(Dmax​) and η=Dmin​/Dmax​. The surface density is the azimuthal average: 2πrΣdr=(πρK/6)Dr3−α​dDr​. It applies at t>0 before removal at the radius in question; the initial state is a delta-function ring. A local angular density needs additional phase information.

Let the initial dust mass be md​, let its differential number distribution be KD−α with α<4 between Dmin​ and Dmax​, and put η=Dmin​/Dmax​. During one dust orbital period, take the stellar direction R and flux at the planet's stellar radius ap​ as constant. The velocity-dependent Poynting–Robertson drag has relative work
⟨ε˙p​⟩=−ap2​A​⟨u2+(u⋅R)2⟩,A=cβGM⋆​​.
(30)
The constant terms have zero work over the closed circular orbit. Since ⟨ui​uj​⟩=(u2/2)(δij​−ki​kj​),

(31)
The coefficient is three for coplanar stellar and dust orbits; it is two for a dust plane normal to the instantaneous stellar direction. Stellar-wind drag is the tangential force exerted by a star's outflow on an orbiting grain. Like Poynting–Robertson drag, it removes orbital energy and angular momentum.

Resonant trapping of dust

Words: 347 Articles: 4
Interplanetary dust OurBigBook.com
During inward migration, dust can be captured into an exterior mean-motion resonance with a planet. A phase-shifted conjunction then lets planetary torque replace angular momentum lost to Poynting–Robertson drag.

Resonant trapping of dust OurBigBook.com
For an exterior (p+1):p mean-motion resonance, use mean longitude in ϕ=(p+1)λ−pλp​−ϖ, z=eexp(iϕ), x=(a−ar​)/ar​ and B=3pnp​/2. Given e˙=−Csinϕ−Ae and ϖ˙=(C/e)cosϕ, the leading Keplerian detuning gives ϕ˙​=−Bx−(C/e)cosϕ. Differentiating z and using eiϕ(sinϕ+icosϕ)=i proves the displayed equation. It retains resonant forcing and eccentricity damping without the coordinate singularity at e=0. True longitude adds a fast orbital ripple and does not yield this autonomous averaged equation directly.
Fixed points of a damped first-order exterior resonance (ef2​=2/[5(p+1)])
Words: 138
Damped first-order resonant complex eccentricity OurBigBook.com
For positive locally constant A,C, supplement damped first-order resonant complex eccentricity by a˙/a=−2(p+1)Cesinϕ−4A/5. Balancing the two dissipative rates gives ef2​=2/[5(p+1)], sinϕf​=−Aef​/C and Bxf​=−(C/ef​)cosϕf​. Two fixed points exist when A<C5(p+1)/2​. The negative-cosine branch has xf​>0 and is stable in this leading model: a phase increase raises the positive resonant torque, raises semi-major axis, lowers mean motion, and reverses the phase drift. The positive-cosine branch has the opposite feedback.
For a coupled verification put z=u+iv. The characteristic polynomial at either fixed point is λ3+2Aλ2+[A2+B2xf2​−2B(p+1)Cuf​]λ−4AB(p+1)Cuf​. For uf​<0 its positive coefficients satisfy the cubic Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion, since the remaining inequality reduces to 2A(A2+B2xf2​)>0. For uf​>0 its negative constant term forces a positive real root. At the equality threshold the equilibria merge and an eigenvalue is zero. This is local stability for the frozen smooth-coefficient approximation, not a conclusion for arbitrary rapidly varying dissipation laws.

dtd(e2)​=a2A​[p+q2q​−p+q5p−q​e2],eeq2​=5p−q2q​,τ=A(5p−q)a2(p+q)​.

For 5p>q, squared orbital eccentricity approaches this equilibrium exponentially in the truncated model. If the predicted value is not small, higher-order terms are needed for quantitative dynamics. Finite planetary torque also imposes a minimum eccentricity for balance, which alone does not guarantee capture during migration.

Pericentre geometry of an exterior resonance

Words: 42
Resonant trapping of dust OurBigBook.com
At pericentre, mean longitude equals longitude of periapsis, so resonant argument ϕ=(p+q)λ−pλp​−qϖ becomes ϕ=p(ϖ−λp​). The pericentre angle in the planet's rotating frame is ϕ/p modulo 2π/p. For coprime p,q, there are p distinct pericentre directions before the trajectory closes. Resonant-argument libration restricts these directions and supplies resonance protection.
